analysis.one_liner: Makes every COVID-era regulatory waiver permanent unless Congress passes a law to restore the rule.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have permanently repealed any federal rule suspended during the COVID-19 emergency unless Congress affirmatively restored it, was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced and never received a hearing or vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During the COVID-19 emergency, federal agencies temporarily waived or modified many rules. Normally, those waivers would end when the emergency ends and the rules would go back into effect. This bill flipped that: every waived or modified rule would be permanently repealed or changed the day the emergency ends, unless a new review commission recommended keeping it and Congress passed a law confirming that recommendation. In other words, protections would disappear by default and come back only by passing brand-new legislation. The bill never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill had passed, the main beneficiaries would have been businesses and other entities whose federal obligations were suspended during the COVID-19 emergency. Any rule an agency had waived — rules that otherwise bind companies on health, safety, environmental, or consumer matters — would have been permanently repealed unless Congress affirmatively passed a law to restore it. That would have let industries keep whatever relief they received during the pandemic indefinitely, without agencies ever having to justify the change through normal rulemaking.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Businesses freed from suspended federal rules

how_it_helps.text: Every rule an agency waived or modified during the COVID emergency would be repealed or modified permanently the day after the emergency ends, without the agency ever having to go through the normal public rulemaking process to make the change.

A rule would be restored only if a new review commission recommended keeping it AND Congress enacted a law confirming that recommendation — two affirmative steps, either of which could block restoration.
Agencies would get one month to report on whether they can function without each suspended rule, with a public comment period, before congressional committees made recommendations.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would have fallen on the people those suspended rules protect: workers, consumers, patients, and communities who rely on federal health, safety, environmental, and consumer regulations. Because the bill made repeal the default, a rule protecting the public would vanish automatically and return only if Congress managed to pass a new law — an extremely high bar, especially during divided government.

drawbacks.text: The bill reversed the normal burden: instead of a waiver simply expiring when the emergency ends, every rule waived during COVID would be repealed by default, and the rule would come back only if Congress passed a brand-new law. In a divided Congress, passing any given law is difficult, so many public protections — workplace, health, and environmental rules — could be permanently lost through inaction.

Not all COVID-era waivers hurt the public. Some flexibilities — such as expanded telehealth rules and other changes that made care and services easier to get during the pandemic — benefited ordinary people. The bill treated every waiver identically and would have swept away the helpful ones along with the harmful ones unless Congress affirmatively acted for each.

The review the bill required was fast and shallow: agencies had one month to report, the review commissions one to two months, and the process required no new analysis of how repealing each rule would affect the people it protected.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill had one real aim: stop temporary emergency rule changes from quietly becoming permanent government power. That is a legitimate concern. But the mechanism was badly designed for ordinary people: it reversed the burden of proof, so protections disappeared by default and came back only by passing a new law — an extraordinarily high bar in a divided Congress. A narrower bill could have reviewed waivers case by case without making repeal the default for every rule the government suspended, including emergency flexibilities that patients, workers, and businesses liked. As written, the potential costs to people who rely on health, safety, and environmental rules outweighed the anti-overreach benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced, neither committee ever took it up, and the Congress ended with no hearing and no vote.

narrative.text: The bill's entire recorded history is two actions on May 1, 2020: introduction and referral to the House Oversight and Reform Committee and the House Judiciary Committee.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote was ever recorded, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The bill attracted only six cosponsors, all House Republicans, during its eight months in Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who rely on federal health, safety, and environmental rules are better off, because the default permanent repeal never happened; the suspended rules remained temporary, as waivers normally are.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People who rely on federal safety and health rules

against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after the May 1, 2020 referral — no hearing, markup, or vote.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all six cosponsors were House Republicans, and no Democrat signed on; no vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.industry: Regulated industries broadly (manufacturing, energy, agriculture, trucking, and other businesses subject to federal rules)
industries.note: Businesses whose obligations were suspended during the COVID emergency would see those suspensions become permanent repeals unless Congress affirmatively passed a law to restore each rule. Rules that protect workers, consumers, and the environment impose costs on the companies they regulate; this bill would default those costs away.

Agencies would lose, by default, any rule they had temporarily waived during the emergency, and would need Congress to pass a law to get a rule back — a reversal of how the normal rulemaking process works. This was a core aim of the bill's sponsor.
